title: How long will it take for Washington fire victims to get FEMA relief?
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
How long will it take for Washington fire victims to get FEMA relief?

Gov. Bob Ferguson submitted a letter to Trump asking him to unlock up to $42,500 for individuals.

Actual Article Body:
Gov. Bob Ferguson submitted a letter to Trump asking him to unlock up to $42,500 for individuals.

Governor Bob Ferguson announced September 28 that he had submitted a letter to President Donald Trump asking for a federal major disaster declaration in the wake of a devastating wildfires across Eastern Washington in late July and early August.

The fires caused more than $188 million in damages, Ferguson said at a Monday press conference in Spokane. A major disaster declaration would open up an estimated $11.2 million in funds for individuals for Benton, Spokane, Stevens and Okanogan counties and the Spokane Tribe of Indians, and qualify the state for an additional $117.7 million in public assistance funds for debris cleanup and emergency costs across 11 counties. Now, the region waits for the president's decision.

A preliminary damage assessment by the Washington State Emergency Management Division, FEMA and local county jurisdictions showed that the fires had burned nearly 369,000 acres. Across the four counties, the fires destroyed 649 primary residences, with an additional 2,542 homes damaged, and forced more than 118,000 people to evacuate. About 70% of affected county residents and Spokane tribal members were insured, Ferguson said.

Ferguson credited Trump for “very quickly” granting the initial emergency declaration that allocated short-term federal resources for immediate response in the wake of the wildfires.

“But to be candid, the most significant request by far that any state has in a situation like this, that any community has in a situation like this, is the one that we're seeking today: a major disaster declaration,” he said.

Over the past five years, across both the Biden and Trump administrations, the president has taken an average of 43 days to approve a request for aid from Washington, according to a RANGE analysis of FEMA data. This encompasses seven approved state declarations and three from tribal nations in Washington.

Approval for the 2023 Gray and Oregon Fires took more than four months. The state's 2025 floods — the most recent major disaster declaration in Washington — took two and a half months to be officially approved.

“I want to emphasize that each disaster declaration request from different states can have its own timeline,” Ferguson said Monday.

Ferguson pointed to how the state had received a major disaster declaration for the historic flooding that more than a dozen counties experienced last December.

He described the federal administration as "tremendously helpful" in past situations.

“I have had multiple communications with folks at the federal level and the administration and deeply appreciate the assistance they provided to us up to this point," Ferguson said.

Jeremy Fagan and his wife Kittie Blansfield lost their home just a couple blocks from Rifle Club Road and are hoping for the funding to come through.

If the disaster declaration is approved, they’re planning to apply for FEMA funds. Ferguson’s request asks for the maximum amount of $42,500 to be made available for FEMA’s Individual Assistance Program.

“I have a whole house to rebuild, so I'll probably apply for the maximum,” Fagan said.

Ferguson’s request detailed that nearly 900,000 acres had burned in Washington this year as of September 2. So far, the state has invested more than $150 million for wildfire response and recovery in 2026 and distributed nearly $1 million in assistance to more than 600 households thus far, according to a press release from Ferguson’s office.

Since 2021, FEMA has committed more than $214 million in approved individual assistance and obligated hazard mitigation and public assistance funding to Washington as the state has grappled with disasters like severe storms, flooding and wildfires.

However, outlets like the New York Times and the Associated Press have reported increased approval times for disaster assistance nationwide in recent months.

Dan Bisbee, the local district director for US
